title: Diogenes and the king
hook: Alexander offers him anything, and the Cynic asks him to stand out of his sunlight

segments.voice: Yesterday: imago vitae, the image of a life, the one gift Seneca had left to give. After three heavy days, a lighter one.
screen: `IMAGO VITAE — THE IMAGE OF A LIFE.`

segments.voice: Corinth, Greece. Alexander, the young king of Macedon, not yet the conqueror he's about to become, comes to town, and everyone important rushes to congratulate him. One man doesn't come. So Alexander goes to find him, lying on the ground in the sun: an old man with a stick, a cloak and almost nothing else. The young king with an army stands over the man who owns nothing, and makes him an offer.
screen: `A YOUNG KING IN CORINTH.` → `EVERYONE RUSHES TO THE KING.` → `ONE MAN STAYS IN THE SUN.`

segments.voice: He was Diogenes of Sinope, the Cynic: one of the dog-like philosophers from Zeno's story, who owned nothing and said what they thought. Crates, the door-opener, is said to have learned from him. Our source is a different Diogenes, Diogenes Laërtius, a biographer writing centuries later. Same name, no relation. Alexander says: ask me for anything you want. Diogenes squints up and says: stand out of my light. That's it. Offered the world, he wanted the sun back. He lived like that on purpose. The stories say he slept in a big clay storage jar, walked around in broad daylight with a lamp, looking for a human being, and, asked where he was from, answered: I'm a citizen of the world. He wasn't always pleasant; the stories are full of rudeness and stunts. But there was a serious point underneath. One way to read this one: much of what people chase is a kind of shade, blocking a simple good already shining on them. And a strange ending. Plutarch says that as Alexander walked away, his officers laughing at the old man, the king said: if I weren't Alexander, I would be Diogenes. Maybe the king saw the one thing an empire couldn't give the Cynic, because he already had it: the light.
screen: `DIOGENES OF SINOPE, THE CYNIC.` · `ASK ME FOR ANYTHING.` · `A LAMP IN BROAD DAYLIGHT.` · `IF I WEREN'T ALEXANDER.` · then, large: `STAND OUT OF MY LIGHT.`

segments.voice: If there's sunlight near you, sit or stand in it; if not, a lamp or the memory of sun on your face will do. Close your eyes and feel the warmth: nothing is being offered, and nothing is needed. When a want or a worry steps in front of it, notice the shade, and let it move aside.
Diogenes. A Cynic philosopher who, offered anything by Alexander the Great, asked only to stand out of his sunlight.
Your line: stand out of my light. Some good things are already shining. Day thirty-four, done.

screen: `DAY 34 COUNTS.` → `TOMORROW: DIOGENES THROWS AWAY HIS CUP.`

howItsDone: The Cynics practiced radical simplicity, living with almost no possessions; some people today borrow a gentler version, cutting back on what they own and chase to make room for simple goods.

fork.setup: you're Diogenes, lying in the sun. Alexander the Great stands over you and says: ask me for anything you want. what do you ask?
options: that he stand out of your light.
fork.reveal: "stand out of my light." the king offered him the world, and what he wanted was the sun back.

original.note: Greek, kosmopolitēs: citizen of the world. Diogenes's answer when asked where he came from, and the root of English cosmopolitan.

trapdoor: what you thought: a rude old man and a funny comeback.
what it means: much of what we chase can block a simple good that's already shining on us.
what a scholar hears: Diogenes Laërtius 6.38 and Plutarch, Alexander 14; the tub was a pithos, a large clay storage jar (DL 6.23), and kosmopolitēs is DL 6.63.

notes: Date and place: Corinth, c. 336–335 BCE, when Alexander was about 20; DL 6.38 places Diogenes sunning himself in the Craneum. Confirm.
Crates as Diogenes's student: DL 6.85–87 says Crates was a pupil of Diogenes (some sources say of Bryson). Confirm.

'Stand out of my light' and 'if I were not Alexander, I would be Diogenes' are paraphrased from DL 6.38 and Plutarch, Alexander 14 (no PD translation on the list); the fork reveal puts the famous phrase in quotation marks as the story's line. Confirm acceptable.
